title: Digestion: the journey of food from mouth to stomach to intestines

summary.text: Bend down until your head is lower than your stomach, and swallow a bite of banana. The bite still reaches your stomach. Food does not fall down inside you. Rings of muscle squeeze it along a food tube that is about 8 metres long in a grown-up. On the way, teeth, acid, bile and other juices break the food into very small pieces. Only pieces that small can pass through the gut wall into the blood. Your child counts chews to find what makes a bite ready to swallow. They also shake oil with soap to see what bile does to fat.
summary.art: A child bending forward with her hands on the floor and her head lower than her stomach, with a dotted line showing a bite of food moving from her mouth up towards her stomach.

intro.hook: An astronaut on the space station floats, and so does her dinner. Nothing falls there. So how does the food she swallows reach her stomach?
intro.text: Many people say that food falls into the stomach. In space nothing falls, yet astronauts eat three meals a day. In this unit you test the idea on your own body. You swallow a bite of banana with your head lower than your stomach. You count your chews to find what makes a bite ready to swallow. You lay out a food tube of wool across the floor. You also shake oil with soap to see how your body deals with fat.
intro.art: An astronaut floating inside a space station with a spoon of food floating in front of her mouth.

outcomes: I can say what digestion is for: breaking food into pieces small enough to pass into the blood.
I can name the parts of the food tube in order, and the two helper organs.
I can explain what chewing and saliva do, and test what makes a bite ready to swallow.
I can explain how peristalsis moves food along the tube, even uphill.
I can explain what the stomach does: it stores, churns, adds acid and lets food out slowly.
I can explain what bile and pancreatic juice do, and how villi absorb digested food.
I can explain what the large intestine and its bacteria do, and what faeces are made of.
I can say how long the food tube is, how long the journey takes, and how people found out.

terms.meaning: Breaking food down into pieces small enough to pass through the gut wall into the blood.
terms.example: The starch in rice is digested into sugar, and the sugar passes into your blood.
terms.art: A grain of rice on the left, an arrow, and many tiny dots passing through a wall on the right.

terms.meaning: The one long tube that food travels through, from the mouth to the anus. Its proper name is the digestive tract.
terms.example: The food pipe, the stomach and the intestines are all parts of the food tube.
terms.art: A simple outline of a child with one continuous tube drawn from the mouth down to the bottom.

terms.meaning: The watery liquid your mouth makes. It wets food and starts to digest starch.
terms.example: Your mouth fills with saliva when you smell hot sambar.
terms.art: A child's open mouth with small drops drawn under the tongue.

terms.meaning: A soft, wet ball of chewed food that is ready to swallow.
terms.example: After you chew a bite of dosa, your tongue rolls it into a bolus.
terms.art: A side view of a mouth with a small round ball of food on the back of the tongue.

terms.meaning: The tube of muscle that carries food from the throat to the stomach. In a grown-up it is about 25 centimetres long.
terms.example: A swallowed bite takes less than 10 seconds to pass down the oesophagus.
terms.art: A side view of a neck and chest with a narrow tube running from the throat to the stomach.

terms.meaning: A wave of squeezing that travels along the food tube. A ring of muscle tightens behind the food and pushes it forward.
terms.example: Peristalsis carries water to your stomach even when your head is down.
terms.art: A tube with a lump inside, pinched narrow just behind the lump, and an arrow showing the lump moving forward.

terms.meaning: A stretchy bag of muscle below the ribs on the left. It stores food, churns it and mixes it with acid.
terms.example: After a full meal a grown-up's stomach holds about 1 litre.
terms.art: A bean-shaped bag with thick walls, a tube entering at the top and another leaving at the bottom.

terms.meaning: A chemical made by living cells that speeds up one kind of change. A digestive enzyme cuts one kind of food molecule into smaller pieces.
terms.example: An enzyme in saliva cuts starch into sugar.
terms.art: A long chain of beads with a small pair of scissors cutting one bead off the end.

terms.meaning: The thick liquid that food becomes after the stomach has churned it with acid.
terms.example: Idli and sambar leave the stomach as chyme, a little at a time.
terms.art: A stomach cut open to show a thick, soupy liquid inside.

terms.meaning: The long, narrow, coiled part of the food tube after the stomach. Most digestion happens here, and nearly all digested food is absorbed here.
terms.example: A grown-up's small intestine is about 6 metres long.
terms.art: A belly outline filled with many loops of a narrow tube.

terms.meaning: A yellow-green liquid made by the liver. It breaks fat into tiny droplets.
terms.example: Bile flows into the small intestine after you eat something oily, such as a vada.
terms.art: A liver with a small green bag under it and a thin tube leading to the small intestine.

terms.meaning: Tiny finger-shaped bumps that cover the inside of the small intestine. Digested food passes through them into the blood. One of them is called a villus.
terms.example: Each villus is about 1 millimetre tall, and there are millions of them.
terms.art: A close view of the inside wall of a tube covered with rows of tiny fingers, like the loops of a towel.

terms.meaning: To take in. The gut wall absorbs digested food and water, and passes them to the blood.
terms.example: The small intestine absorbs sugar. The large intestine absorbs water.
terms.art: Small dots passing from the inside of a tube, through its wall, into a red blood vessel.

terms.meaning: The wider, shorter last part of the food tube. It takes back water, and it is home to trillions of bacteria.
terms.example: A grown-up's large intestine is about 1.5 metres long.
terms.art: A wide tube that runs up, across and down around the edges of a belly, like a frame around the coiled small intestine.

terms.meaning: The solid waste that leaves the body through the anus. It is also called stool or poo.
terms.example: Faeces are about three quarters water. Much of the rest is bacteria and fibre.
terms.art: A simple toilet seen from the side, with a label line pointing down into the bowl.

explanations.definition: Digestion means breaking food down into pieces small enough to pass through the gut wall into the blood.
explanations.description: Your body cannot use a piece of idli as it is. The piece is far too big to enter the blood. Food is made of molecules, which are tiny particles too small to see. Many food molecules are long chains. Starch is a chain of thousands of sugar units. A protein is a chain of units called amino acids. Fat is made of smaller units too. Digestion cuts these chains into single units, and only those units can cross the gut wall. The body breaks food in two ways. Teeth and muscles break it by force into smaller pieces. This is called mechanical digestion. Enzymes break it by chemistry into smaller molecules. This is called chemical digestion. An enzyme is a chemical made by cells that cuts one kind of molecule. Water, salt and vitamins are already small, so they need no digesting.
examples: Starch from rice is cut into sugar.
Protein from dal or egg is cut into amino acids.
Fat from groundnut oil is cut into smaller units called fatty acids.
explanations.art: A long chain of beads on the left being cut by scissors into single beads, and the single beads passing through a wall on the right.

explanations.concept: The mouth: teeth, saliva and the bolus
explanations.definition: In the mouth, teeth break food into small pieces and saliva wets it. The tongue rolls the wet pieces into a soft ball called a bolus.
explanations.description: Chewing does two jobs. The first job is breaking. Front teeth cut the bite, and back teeth grind it. Small pieces have more surface for the juices to work on. The second job is wetting. Three pairs of glands make saliva, about 1 litre every day. Saliva makes the pieces slippery and sticks them together. It also holds an enzyme called amylase, which begins to cut starch into sugar. A bite is ready to swallow only when the pieces are small and also wet enough to hold together. A dry biscuit breaks easily but needs many chews, because the mouth has to add water. A raw carrot is wet inside but needs many chews, because the pieces are hard to break.
examples: A bite of dry rusk needs many chews. A bite of rusk dipped in tea needs few.
Chew plain cooked rice slowly, and after a minute it begins to taste a little sweet.
Your mouth waters when you smell lemon pickle, before you eat any.
explanations.art: A side view of a mouth with the front teeth cutting a piece of food and drops of saliva falling on it.

explanations.definition: Peristalsis is a wave of squeezing that travels along the food tube. A ring of muscle tightens just behind the food and pushes it forward.
explanations.description: When you swallow, the tongue pushes the bolus to the back of the mouth. A small flap called the epiglottis folds over the top of the windpipe. This keeps food out of the lungs. For that moment you stop breathing. The bolus enters the oesophagus, the food pipe. In a grown-up the oesophagus is about 25 centimetres long. Its wall is muscle. A ring of muscle tightens behind the bolus, and the ring in front relaxes. The tightening moves along the tube as a wave. The bolus reaches the stomach in less than 10 seconds. Food is pushed along by muscle. It is not pulled down by gravity, so it does not matter which way your head points. You can swallow with your head down. Astronauts swallow in space, where nothing falls. A cow drinks with her head far below her shoulders. Peristalsis does not stop at the stomach. It moves food along the whole tube, to the very end.
examples: An astronaut eats a meal while floating.
A cow with her head down at a trough swallows water up along her neck.
A snake moves a whole egg along the body by squeezing behind it.
explanations.art: A tube drawn three times, with a lump of food further along each time and the tube pinched narrow just behind the lump.

explanations.concept: The stomach: store, churn, add acid, let out slowly
explanations.definition: The stomach is a stretchy bag of muscle. It stores a meal and churns it with acid and enzymes. Then it lets the meal out into the small intestine a little at a time.
explanations.description: An empty stomach is about as big as a fist. After a full meal a grown-up's stomach stretches to hold about 1 litre. A ring of muscle at the top closes, so food does not go back up. The stomach wall has three layers of muscle, and it squeezes about three times a minute. Glands in the wall make gastric juice. This juice holds hydrochloric acid, which is about as strong as the acid in lemon juice or stronger. The acid kills many microbes that were swallowed with the food. Gastric juice also holds an enzyme called pepsin, which starts to cut proteins. After 2 to 4 hours the meal has become a thick liquid called chyme. A ring of muscle at the stomach's exit opens a little, again and again. Each time, a spoonful or so of chyme passes into the small intestine. The stomach does not digest its own wall, because the wall is coated with thick, slippery mucus. The cells of the lining are also replaced every few days.
examples: Your stomach feels tight after a wedding feast because its wall has stretched.
A burp is swallowed air coming back up from the stomach.
A stomach growls when its muscles squeeze gas and liquid along.
explanations.art: A stomach cut open to show folds in its wall, a thick liquid inside, a closed ring at the top and a small opening at the bottom.

explanations.concept: The small intestine: where most digestion happens
explanations.definition: The small intestine is a narrow tube about 6 metres long in a grown-up. Most chemical digestion happens in it.
explanations.description: Many people think the stomach does most of the digesting. The small intestine does far more. It is called small because it is narrow, about 2.5 centimetres wide. The chyme from the stomach is sour with acid. In the first part of the small intestine, two juices are added through a small tube. One is bile. The liver makes bile, and a small bag called the gall bladder stores it. Bile is not an enzyme. It works the way dish soap works on a greasy plate. It breaks large drops of fat into tiny droplets, so that enzymes can reach the fat. The other juice comes from the pancreas, an organ behind the stomach. Pancreatic juice holds enzymes for starch, protein and fat. It also holds a base, which cancels the stomach's acid. The wall of the small intestine adds enzymes of its own. Food never passes through the liver or the pancreas. They are helper organs, and they send their juices in. Food spends 3 to 5 hours in the small intestine.
examples: After a meal with ghee, the gall bladder squeezes bile into the small intestine.
Starch that saliva did not finish is cut into sugar by pancreatic juice.
A person whose stomach has been removed by surgeons can still digest food.
explanations.art: A stomach leading into a looped tube, with a liver and a small green bag above and a pancreas behind, joined to the tube by one small pipe.

explanations.concept: Absorption: how digested food enters the blood
explanations.definition: To absorb means to take in. The wall of the small intestine absorbs digested food and passes it into the blood.
explanations.description: The inside of the small intestine is not smooth. It has folds, and the folds are covered with millions of tiny fingers called villi. Each villus is about 1 millimetre tall. The cells on each villus have even smaller bumps of their own. All this folding gives the lining a very large surface. A smooth tube of the same size would have about half a square metre. The real lining has about 30 square metres, as much as the floors of three small bedrooms. Inside every villus are tiny blood vessels. Sugars and amino acids pass through the wall of the villus into this blood. Fats pass into a nearby set of vessels called lymph vessels, and join the blood later. The blood from the intestine goes first to the liver. The liver stores some sugar, changes some molecules and breaks down many harmful ones. Then the blood carries the food to every cell of the body.
examples: Sugar from a banana can be in your blood within about 15 minutes.
A child with loose motions is given a drink of sugar, salt and water. The sugar helps the gut absorb the salt and the water.
A terry towel soaks up more water than a flat cloth, because its loops give it more surface.
explanations.art: A close view of three finger-shaped villi with red and blue blood vessels inside them and small dots moving from the gut into the vessels.

explanations.concept: The large intestine: water, bacteria and faeces
explanations.definition: The large intestine is a wide tube about 1.5 metres long in a grown-up. It takes back water and salts, and it is home to trillions of bacteria.
explanations.description: What reaches the large intestine is watery. It holds fibre, which is the part of plants that human enzymes cannot cut. It also holds water, salts and worn-out cells from the gut lining. Each day the body pours about 7 litres of juices into the food tube. Nearly all of that water is absorbed again, most of it in the small intestine and the rest here. Tens of trillions of bacteria live in the large intestine. They feed on the fibre. They make some vitamins, such as vitamin K, and some gases. The leftovers move slowly and stay for 1 to 2 days. What remains is faeces. Faeces are about three quarters water. Much of the solid part is bacteria, and the rest is mostly fibre. The brown colour comes from bile. Faeces are stored in the last part, the rectum, and leave through the anus. This last step is one that you control.
examples: After eating plenty of vegetables and whole grains, faeces are soft and bulky, because fibre holds water.
With loose motions, food moves too fast, so too little water is absorbed.
Gas passed from the bottom is made mostly by gut bacteria.
explanations.art: A wide tube framing a belly on three sides, and a magnified circle beside the tube showing tiny rod-shaped bacteria.

explanations.concept: The whole journey: how far and how long
explanations.definition: The food tube of a grown-up is about 8 metres long from the top of the oesophagus to the anus. A meal usually takes between 1 and 3 days to pass through.
explanations.description: Add up the parts. The oesophagus is about 25 centimetres. The stomach is about 25 centimetres. The small intestine is about 6 metres. The large intestine is about 1.5 metres. Together they make about 8 metres. A child's food tube is shorter, because a child is smaller. These lengths differ from one person to another. They are also hard to measure in a living body, because the muscles of the tube keep it pulled short. The times differ too. A bite spends less than 10 seconds in the oesophagus. It spends 2 to 4 hours in the stomach and 3 to 5 hours in the small intestine. It spends 1 to 2 days in the large intestine. So the fastest part of the journey is the first, and the slowest is the last. Fatty meals leave the stomach more slowly than meals of rice or fruit.
examples: A skin of sweetcorn swallowed at dinner often appears in the faeces one or two days later.
A drink of water leaves the stomach in minutes, but a meal with fried food stays for hours.
The small intestine makes up about three quarters of the length of the tube.
explanations.art: A long strip divided into four parts of different lengths, labelled oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine, with a clock above each part.

explanations.definition: The wall of the food tube holds a net of hundreds of millions of nerve cells. This net is called the enteric nervous system, and it runs digestion.
explanations.description: You decide when to swallow, and you decide when to go to the toilet. Everything between those two moments happens without your deciding. In 1899 two English scientists, William Bayliss and Ernest Starling, studied the intestine of a dog. They found that it squeezes behind a lump of food and relaxes in front of it. It went on doing this after its nerves to the brain were cut. So the intestine senses the food and moves it by its own nerve net. This net is sometimes called the second brain. The gut and the brain also send messages to each other all day. Most travel along the vagus nerve. That is how you feel hungry, full or sick. It is also why a fright before an exam can upset your stomach. The gut sends chemical messages too. In 1902 Bayliss and Starling found that the small intestine releases a chemical into the blood when acid touches it. The chemical tells the pancreas to pour out juice. Starling later named such messengers hormones.
examples: An empty stomach growls about every one and a half to two hours. Waves of squeezing are sweeping the leftovers along.
Your mouth waters and your stomach starts making juice when you only smell food.
You feel 'butterflies' in your belly before going on stage.
explanations.art: A piece of intestine with a fine net of nerve cells drawn in its wall, and one long nerve running up from it to a brain.

explanations.concept: Do the microbes in your gut affect how you feel?
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that gut bacteria help digest fibre and make some vitamins. They disagree about how much gut bacteria affect mood and behaviour.
explanations.description: Tens of trillions of bacteria live in the large intestine. That is about as many as the cells of your own body. They make many chemicals, and some of these reach the nerves of the gut and the blood. Scientists are testing whether these chemicals change how animals, including humans, feel and act.
examples: Mice raised with no microbes at all behave differently from ordinary mice.
Some people feel low when their gut is upset, and some feel sick when they are worried.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study mice, such as Rochellys Diaz Heijtz and her team in Sweden in 2011
perspectives.explanation: Mice raised without any microbes moved about more and were less cautious than ordinary mice. Giving them microbes early in life changed this. So gut microbes can shape a growing brain, at least in mice.
A mouse with no microbes at all is very unlike any human. Studies in people are small and often disagree. We do not yet know whether changing gut bacteria changes a person's mood.

explanations.art: A mouse on one side and a child on the other, each with a small circle showing gut bacteria and a dotted line from the belly to the brain.

agreed.text: Digestion is chemical as well as mechanical. Juices change food, and grinding alone does not explain it.
agreed.evidence: In 1752 René de Réaumur fed a kite small metal tubes with meat inside. The tubes could not be crushed, yet the meat came back partly dissolved.

agreed.text: The stomach makes an acid juice that dissolves meat, and it churns food as it does so.
agreed.evidence: From 1825 to 1833 William Beaumont watched digestion through a hole in the stomach of Alexis St. Martin. He took out gastric juice and saw it digest meat in a glass tube kept warm.

agreed.text: Food is moved along the tube by waves of squeezing, and the gut's own nerves run them.
agreed.evidence: In 1896 and 1897 Walter Cannon, then a medical student, used the newly found X-rays. He watched food move in living animals. In 1899 Bayliss and Starling showed the intestine still does this with its nerves to the brain cut.

agreed.text: Most digestion and nearly all absorption of food happen in the small intestine.
agreed.evidence: People whose stomachs have been removed can live and digest food. People who lose most of the small intestine cannot absorb enough, and need special feeding.

agreed.text: The lining of the small intestine has a surface of about 30 square metres.
agreed.evidence: In 2014 Herbert Helander and Lars Fändriks measured folds, villi and the bumps on cells under microscopes. Their figure is much smaller than the 'tennis court' that older books give.

agreed.text: Sugar helps the small intestine absorb salt and water.
agreed.evidence: In 1971 Dr Dilip Mahalanabis and his team worked in refugee camps near Bangaon in West Bengal. They gave people with cholera a drink of sugar and salt. Far fewer of them died than of those treated in the usual way.

challenging.claim: Food falls down into the stomach, so you must sit up to swallow.
challenging.for: We usually eat sitting up, and things do fall downwards.
challenging.against: Food is pushed by peristalsis. People swallow with the head down, and astronauts swallow where nothing falls. Sitting up is still wise, because it makes choking less likely.

challenging.claim: The stomach does most of the digesting.
challenging.who: Many people, and the everyday meaning of the word 'stomach'.
challenging.for: The stomach is where we feel a meal, and its acid is strong.
challenging.against: The stomach mainly stores, churns and starts on protein. Most digestion and nearly all absorption happen in the small intestine.

challenging.claim: Stomach ulcers come from worry and spicy food.
challenging.for: Ulcer pain often gets worse with worry and with some foods.
challenging.against: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren in Australia found a bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, in the stomachs of ulcer patients. In 1984 Marshall drank the bacteria and his stomach became inflamed. Most ulcers are caused by this bacterium or by some pain medicines. They won the Nobel Prize in 2005.

challenging.claim: Swallowed chewing gum stays in the stomach for seven years.
challenging.for: Gum base is not digested by any human enzyme.
challenging.against: Peristalsis moves gum along like any other thing that is not digested. It leaves in the faeces within a few days.

challenging.claim: The appendix is a useless leftover.
challenging.who: Many biology books of the last century.
challenging.for: People live well after the appendix is removed.
challenging.against: In 2007 William Parker's team at Duke University proposed that the appendix is a safe store of helpful bacteria. After an illness empties the gut, the appendix can supply bacteria to fill the gut again. The idea is not yet proven.

challenging.claim: The inside of the food tube is outside the body.
challenging.who: Many biologists who study how bodies are built.
challenging.for: The tube is open at both ends. A swallowed seed can pass through without crossing any wall of the body.
challenging.against: The gut is plainly an organ inside the belly. The body pours juices into it and controls what happens there. It is true that the tube is open to the outside at both ends. But saying the inside of the gut is outside the body can mislead.

big_questions.q: A swallowed sweetcorn skin passes through you and comes out unchanged. Was the skin ever inside you?
big_questions.hint: Think about a marble rolling through a pipe. Is the marble inside the pipe's wall?

big_questions.q: At what moment does a bite of banana stop being banana and start being you?
big_questions.hint: Is it when you swallow, when the sugar crosses the gut wall, or when a cell uses it?

big_questions.q: Your gut runs most of digestion without your deciding. Who is doing that work?
big_questions.hint: The gut has hundreds of millions of nerve cells of its own. Are they part of 'you'?

big_questions.q: Tens of trillions of bacteria live in your large intestine and eat with you. Is a meal eaten by one being or by many?
big_questions.hint: They digest fibre that your own enzymes cannot cut, and they make vitamins you use.

big_questions.q: A cow, a snake and you all move food by peristalsis. Why might such different animals share one way of doing it?
big_questions.hint: Think about what animals had in common long ago, before there were cows, snakes or humans.

big_questions.q: Alexis St. Martin did not choose to have a hole in his stomach. Who should get the credit for what was learned through it?
big_questions.hint: Dr Beaumont did the tests and wrote the book. St. Martin's body made them possible, and he bore the pain.

story.title: The Lump That Climbed
story.note: Kayal, Senthil, Paati and the cow Lakshmi are made up. These facts are real: on Mattu Pongal in Tamil Nadu, families bathe their cattle and paint their horns. A cow swallows grass quickly and later brings it back up, a mouthful at a time, to chew again. That mouthful is called the cud, and you can see it travel up the left side of her neck. Cows drink with their heads down. The stalk of a papaya leaf is hollow, and children do use it as a straw.
text: On the morning of Mattu Pongal, Kayal's cousin Senthil said something that sounded right. Kayal was sure it was wrong, but she could not show it.
They were eating pongal on the thinnai, the raised ledge at the front of Paati's house near Melur. Kayal had leaned back against a pillar with her banana leaf on her lap.
"Sit up straight," said Senthil. He was eleven, and he liked to know things. "Food falls into your stomach like a stone into a well. If you lean back, it gets stuck in your neck."
Kayal swallowed. "Nothing got stuck," she said.
"That is because your neck is still higher than your stomach. Try it with your head lower than your stomach. You cannot do it. Nobody can. If you can, I will give you my piece of sugarcane."
Kayal wanted the sugarcane. But she had never swallowed anything with her head down, and she did not like to lose. "By this evening," she said.
"Done," said Senthil.

In the yard, Paati was painting the horns of Lakshmi the cow, one blue and one yellow. Lakshmi lay under the neem tree with her legs folded, chewing. She had not taken a bite of anything since sunrise. Yet her jaw went round and round.
"Paati, what is she chewing? Her mouth was empty a minute ago."
"Watch her neck," said Paati. "The left side. Do not blink."

Lakshmi swallowed, and her jaw stopped. For a moment nothing happened. Then a lump as big as a lemon appeared low on her neck, near her chest. The lump travelled up under the skin, all the way to her jaw. Her cheek filled, and she began to chew again.
"It went up," said Kayal.
"Every cow does this," said Paati. "She swallows her grass quickly in the morning. Later she brings it back, one mouthful at a time, and chews it properly. That mouthful is called the cud."
"But how does it come up? Nothing falls upwards."

Paati put down her brush. She pulled Thatha's old shirt off the clothes line and took a lemon from the plate beside the paint. She dropped the lemon into one sleeve at the shoulder, and held the sleeve out level.

"I will not tip it," she said. She closed her fingers around the sleeve just behind the lemon, and squeezed. The lemon slid forward. She squeezed behind it again, and again, and the lemon dropped out at the cuff. Then she put it back in at the cuff and squeezed from that side. The lemon went back the way it had come.

"A cow's food pipe is a tube of muscle," said Paati. "So is yours. A ring of the tube squeezes just behind the food. Then the next ring squeezes, and then the next. The food goes where the squeezing sends it. Down, up or along."
Kayal looked across at Senthil, who was tying bells to a calf's rope. She said nothing yet. She wanted to be sure.

In the afternoon her uncle led Lakshmi to the stone trough beside the well. The trough was low, almost at the ground. Lakshmi spread her front legs a little and put her head right down. Her mouth was far below her shoulders.
Kayal crouched and watched the neck. One gulp after another ran along it, from the mouth up towards the chest. The water was climbing.
Now she was sure.

She cut a leaf stalk from the papaya tree behind the kitchen. The stalk was hollow and as long as her forearm. She filled a steel tumbler with thin buttermilk and set it on the ground below the thinnai. Then she called Senthil.
She lay on her stomach on the thinnai, with her head and shoulders hanging over the edge. Her plait fell forward and touched the ground. Her head was lower than her stomach, and anyone could see it.
She put the stalk into the tumbler, sucked, and swallowed.
She felt the cool buttermilk leave the back of her tongue. She felt it travel along her throat and into her chest. She took three more swallows. Then she sat up, red in the face.
"That is a trick," said Senthil. "The straw did it."
"The straw only brings it to my mouth. After that I swallow, the same as Lakshmi." She held out the stalk. "You try."
Senthil lay down and hung his head over the edge. He sucked, and he swallowed. He stayed there a moment, very still.
"It went up," he said.
"It was squeezed up," said Kayal. "The tube does it. Ask Lakshmi."
He gave her the sugarcane without a word. She broke it across her knee and handed him the smaller half.

They sat on the thinnai and chewed. Neither of them spoke. Each was paying attention to the same thing: the moment at the back of the tongue when you let go, and something else carries the food on from there.
story.epiphany: Senthil was sure that food falls into the stomach. Kayal saw a lump of cud climb a cow's neck, and saw water climb the same way. Food is pushed along by rings of muscle, so it can travel in any direction.
ask: Nothing was lifting the cud. So why could the cud travel up the cow's neck?
Senthil said the straw did the work. What did the straw do, and what did the food pipe do?
After you swallow, can you stop the bite halfway down? What does that tell you?
