games.title: Where Is the Bite Now? The journey cards
games.context: This is a card game about the journey of food. Each card says what is happening to a bite. You say which part of the food tube the bite is in.

setup.art: Twenty cards in a shuffled pile on a table, with five small tokens marked Mouth, Food pipe, Stomach, Small intestine and Large intestine in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while another player slides one token forward, face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the front. Everyone else puts down one token, face down.

setup.art: The tokens turned face up and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the back.

printables.title: 20 journey cards: what is happening on the front, the place and the reason on the back

items.f: Front teeth cut me off the dosa, and back teeth grind me.
items.b: Mouth. Teeth break food into small pieces. This is mechanical digestion.

items.f: A watery liquid wets me and starts to cut my starch into sugar.
items.b: Mouth. The liquid is saliva, and its enzyme is amylase.

items.f: A tongue rolls me into a soft, wet ball.
items.b: Mouth. The ball is called a bolus, and it is ready to swallow.

items.f: A flap folds over the windpipe as I pass.
items.b: Food pipe. The flap is the epiglottis. It keeps food out of the lungs as the food pipe takes the bolus.

items.f: A ring of muscle squeezes behind me, in a tube about 25 centimetres long.
items.b: Food pipe. Its proper name is the oesophagus, and the squeezing is peristalsis.

items.f: I pass through this part in less than 10 seconds.
items.b: Food pipe. It is the fastest part of the journey.

items.f: A ring of muscle shuts above me, so I do not go back up.
items.b: Stomach. The ring at the top of the stomach closes after the food comes in.

items.f: Thick walls of muscle squeeze me about three times a minute.
items.b: Stomach. The thick muscle walls squeeze and churn the food.

items.f: An acid about as strong as lemon juice pours over me.
items.b: Stomach. Gastric juice holds hydrochloric acid, which kills many microbes.

items.f: I have become a thick liquid called chyme. I wait here for 2 to 4 hours.
items.b: Stomach. The stomach lets chyme out into the small intestine a little at a time.

items.f: A yellow-green liquid breaks my fat into tiny droplets.
items.b: Small intestine. The liquid is bile, made by the liver.

items.f: A juice from the pancreas cancels the acid around me.
items.b: Small intestine. Pancreatic juice holds a base, and enzymes too.

items.f: I am in a narrow tube about 6 metres long.
items.b: Small intestine. It is the longest part of the food tube.

items.f: Millions of tiny fingers stand all around me.
items.b: Small intestine. The fingers are villi.

items.f: My sugar passes through a wall into the blood.
items.b: Small intestine. Nearly all digested food is absorbed here.

items.f: Blood carries me from here to the liver first.
items.b: Small intestine. Blood from the villi goes to the liver before the rest of the body.

items.f: Water is being taken back from me, and I am getting firmer.
items.b: Large intestine. It absorbs water and salts.

items.f: Trillions of bacteria feed on my fibre.
items.b: Large intestine. The bacteria also make gases and vitamin K.

items.f: I move very slowly here, for 1 to 2 days.
items.b: Large intestine. It is the slowest part of the journey.

items.f: I am stored in the last part until the body is ready to let me go.
items.b: Large intestine. The last part is the rectum, and what leaves is faeces.

printables.title: 5 place tokens: Mouth, Food pipe, Stomach, Small intestine, Large intestine. Print one set for each player

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts one place token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the place on the back scores 1 point.
A player who also says why scores 1 more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone? Read a card, say the place aloud, then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right place.
After all 20 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 20 is your result.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player one set of five tokens.
flow.say: Each card is spoken by a bite of food. The bite says what is happening to it. Your five tokens are the five places a bite passes through.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take five tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Is the Bite Now. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first ten cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card five.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Choose a token and put it face down. Now turn it over. The reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick a place token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: How did you decide which place the card describes?
good: I asked whether the food was being broken, mixed or absorbed.
Acid means the stomach.
Villi and bile belong to the small intestine.

flow.parent: For a stuck child, ask: is the bite being broken, mixed with a juice, absorbed or dried out? One child can play alone or with you.
flow.context: In this step of Where Is the Bite Now you play the first ten journey cards.

flow.do: Play the last ten cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Ten more cards. This time, also try to say why. A good reason earns one more point.
flow.kid: Play ten more cards. Say the reason for each place.
flow.context: In this step of Where Is the Bite Now you play the last ten cards and give reasons.

flow.do: Count the points. Then lay all 20 cards in a line, in the order a bite would meet them.
flow.say: Let us lay the cards in the order of the journey, from the mouth to the end. Which place has the most cards about absorbing?
flow.kid: Lay the cards in journey order. Where is food absorbed?

check.q: In which part is nearly all digested food absorbed into the blood?
check.why: The villi of the small intestine absorb sugars, amino acids and fats. If you chose the stomach, remember that the stomach mainly stores and churns. The large intestine absorbs water and salts.

flow.context: This is the last step of Where Is the Bite Now. You lay the journey cards in order from mouth to large intestine.

games.title: Mouth to Exit: the absorbing game
games.context: This is a board game about the journey of food. You travel the food tube as a bite. You collect a bean each time the body absorbs something from you.

setup.art: A paper board with 30 numbered squares in a winding line, coloured in five zones, with a bowl of beans and a die beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw or print the board of 30 squares. Put about 60 beans in a bowl.

setup.art: Two buttons on square 1 of the board and a child rolling a die.
setup.caption: 2. Put a button for each player on square 1. Roll the die.

setup.art: A child's button on a small intestine square, and her hand taking two beans from the bowl.
setup.caption: 3. If your turn ends in the small intestine, take 2 beans. In the large intestine, take 1.

printables.title: 30 squares in a winding line, from Mouth to Exit. Copy each line into one square
items: 1. MOUTH. Start here. Teeth cut and grind you.
2. MOUTH. You were chewed 20 times and you are soft and wet. Move ahead 1.
3. FOOD PIPE. A flap covers the windpipe as you pass.
4. FOOD PIPE. A ring of muscle squeezes behind you. Move ahead 1.
5. STOMACH. The ring at the top shuts behind you.
7. STOMACH. The stomach churns you for hours. Miss your next turn.
8. STOMACH. You are now a thick liquid called chyme.
9. STOMACH EXIT RING. Everyone stops here. The ring lets food through a little at a time.
10. SMALL INTESTINE. Juice from the pancreas cancels your acid.
12. SMALL INTESTINE. Bile breaks your fat into tiny droplets. Take 1 extra bean.
14. SMALL INTESTINE. Enzymes cut your starch into sugar.
15. SMALL INTESTINE. Villi stand all around you. Take 2 extra beans.
17. SMALL INTESTINE. A harmful microbe! The gut rushes everything along. Give back 2 beans and go to square 24.
19. SMALL INTESTINE. The last sugars and amino acids are absorbed.
20. LARGE INTESTINE. You are watery, and you move slowly now.
22. LARGE INTESTINE. Fibre from vegetables keeps things moving. Move ahead 2.
24. LARGE INTESTINE. Water is taken back into the blood.
26. LARGE INTESTINE. Bacteria make vitamin K from your leftovers. Take 1 extra bean.
28. LARGE INTESTINE. You are firm now. You are faeces.
29. RECTUM. You wait here until the body is ready.
30. EXIT. The first player here takes 3 extra beans.

printables.title: Score sheet: one row for each player, to write the beans counted at the end
items: Beans from the small intestine and large intestine

rules: You need a die, a button for each player and about 60 beans, such as rajma or tamarind seeds. If you have no die, write 1 to 6 on six paper slips and draw one from a tumbler.
Each bean stands for food or water that the body has absorbed from you. The player with the most beans at the end wins.
On your turn, roll the die. Then choose: move the full number, or move just 1 square.
Everyone stops on square 9, the stomach's exit ring, even if the roll would carry them past it.
If your turn ends on a small intestine square, 10 to 19, take 2 beans. If it ends on a large intestine square, 20 to 29, take 1 bean. The mouth, food pipe and stomach give no beans.
If you land on a square with an instruction, follow it. Take the beans for the square where your turn finally ends.
The first player to reach square 30 takes 3 extra beans. Every other player then has one more turn, and the game ends.
Playing alone? You have 14 turns. Count your beans, and lose 5 if you have not reached square 30. Then try to beat your score.

flow.do: Draw the board on a large sheet, or print it. Colour the five zones. Put the beans in a bowl and a button for each player on square 1.
flow.say: You are a bite of food. Beans are what the body absorbs from you. Where on this board do you think the most beans are given?
flow.kid: Draw the board. Put your button on square 1. Where will most beans come from?
flow.context: This is the first step of Mouth to Exit. You set up the board, the buttons and the beans.

flow.do: Play the game by the rules. Read each instruction square aloud when someone lands on it.
flow.say: Roll, then choose. You may move the full number or just one square. Moving slowly earns more beans. But the first to the exit earns three, and then the game ends.
flow.kid: Roll the die. Move the full number or just 1. Collect your beans.

ask.q: Why do the mouth, food pipe and stomach give no beans?
good: Hardly anything is absorbed there.
The food is still being broken down.
Absorbing happens through the villi of the small intestine.

flow.parent: The choice each turn is the heart of the game. A player who races to the exit ends the game while slow players are still collecting.
flow.context: In this step of Mouth to Exit you play the board game and collect beans for absorbed food.

flow.do: Count the beans. Talk about square 17 and about the question below.
flow.say: Count your beans. Look at square 17. The harmful microbe made the gut rush, and the player lost beans. What does that tell us about loose motions?
flow.kid: Count your beans. What happened on square 17? Why did you lose beans?

check.q: Why is a child with loose motions given extra water with sugar and salt?
options: The gut had too little time to absorb water
The stomach made too much acid
The teeth did not chew enough
check.why: With loose motions, food and water rush through, so the body absorbs too little and loses water and salts. If you chose acid or chewing, remember square 17: the loss came from speed.

flow.context: This is the last step of Mouth to Exit. You count the beans and talk about why rushing through the gut loses food and water.

experiments.title: Dry or Wet: what makes a bite ready to swallow?
experiments.question: How many chews does a bite need before you can swallow it? Does dipping the bite in water first change the number? Is the answer the same for a biscuit and for a raw carrot?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which of the four bites will need the most chews, and which the fewest? Will dipping in water help the biscuit, the carrot, both or neither? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use half a plain biscuit for every biscuit bite. Cut every carrot piece to the same size, about as big as the top joint of your thumb. Dip for the same time, a slow count of three. Chew in your usual way, and stop counting when the bite feels ready to swallow. Take a sip of water and wait half a minute between bites. Then your mouth starts the same each time. Do every kind of bite twice. Only two things change: the food, and whether it was dipped.

materials.item: plain biscuits, such as Marie biscuits, or 2 rusks broken into four pieces
raw carrot, washed and peeled (or a piece of raw coconut or a firm guava)
a knife, for the grown-up to cut the carrot
a small bowl of drinking water for dipping, and a tumbler of water for sips
a notebook page and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the carrot. Sit up straight while you chew, and do not talk or laugh with food in your mouth. Do not use nuts, in case of an allergy.
experiments.record: Draw a table with four rows: dry biscuit, dipped biscuit, dry carrot and dipped carrot. Write the number of chews for try 1 and try 2 in each row.
experiments.context: In this experiment you count how many chews a bite needs before it is ready to swallow. You compare a biscuit and a raw carrot, each dry and each dipped in water.

setup.art: Four half biscuits and four small pieces of raw carrot on a steel plate, beside a small bowl of water.
setup.caption: 1. Break 2 biscuits into 4 halves. A grown-up cuts 4 carrot pieces of the same size.

setup.art: A child chewing with one finger raised for each chew, while a grown-up writes in a notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Chew the dry bite in your usual way. Count every chew until the bite is ready to swallow.

setup.art: A child's hand holding half a biscuit in a small bowl of water.
setup.caption: 3. Dip the next bite in water for a slow count of three. Then chew and count.

setup.art: A notebook table with four rows and two columns of numbers.
setup.caption: 4. Do each kind of bite twice. Write down every count.

flow.do: Put the biscuits, the carrot and the bowl of water on the table. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will count the chews for four kinds of bite. They are a dry biscuit, a dipped biscuit, a dry carrot and a dipped carrot. Which will need the most chews? Will dipping help both foods? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the four bites. Which needs the most chews? Will dipping help? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think dipping will or will not help?
good: Water makes the biscuit soft.
A carrot is hard, so water will not change it.
A wet bite slides down more easily.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Dry or Wet. You guess how many chews each bite will need, before you test.

flow.do: Break 2 biscuits into 4 halves. Cut 4 carrot pieces, each about as big as the top joint of your child's thumb. Draw the table with four rows.
flow.say: I will cut the carrot. All four pieces must be the same size. Why does the size matter?
flow.kid: Break the biscuits in half. A grown-up cuts the carrot. Draw the table.
flow.parent: A bigger piece needs more chews, so equal pieces keep the test fair.
flow.context: In this step of Dry or Wet you prepare four half biscuits and four carrot pieces of the same size.

flow.do: Your child eats one dry half biscuit, chewing in the usual way. They raise a finger for each chew, or you count aloud. Stop counting when the bite feels ready to swallow. Write the number. After a sip of water and half a minute, do the dipped half biscuit. Then repeat both.
flow.say: Chew as you always do, and I will count. Raise your hand when the bite feels ready to swallow. Then swallow. Now sip some water and rest your mouth for half a minute.
flow.kid: Chew the dry biscuit and count. Sip water. Then chew the dipped biscuit and count.

check.q: In Dry or Wet, why do you sip water and wait between bites?
options: So my mouth starts the same each time
check.why: A dry bite uses up saliva. If the next bite began with a dry mouth, the test would not be fair. If you chose taste or speed, remember that a fair test changes only one thing at a time.

flow.parent: Dip for a slow count of three. A longer dip turns a biscuit to mush that needs no chewing at all.
flow.context: In this step of Dry or Wet you count the chews for a half biscuit, dry and dipped.

flow.do: Do the same with the carrot: one dry piece, then one piece dipped for a count of three. Then repeat both. Write every count.
flow.say: Now the carrot. Chew in your usual way and count again. Raise your hand when the bite is ready.
flow.kid: Chew the dry carrot and count. Then the dipped carrot. Do both twice.
flow.context: In this step of Dry or Wet you count the chews for a raw carrot piece, dry and dipped.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your eight numbers. Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it happened. Did dipping change the biscuit and the carrot by the same amount?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you found. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Why did dipping help the biscuit so much more than the carrot?
good: The biscuit was dry, and the water did the wetting.
The carrot was already wet inside, but it still had to be broken.
The two foods need different work from the mouth.

ask.q: What two things must be true before a bite can be swallowed?
good: The pieces must be small.
The pieces must be wet enough to stick together and slide.

flow.parent: In most mouths the dipped biscuit needs about half as many chews as the dry one, or fewer. The carrot hardly changes. Write down what you really found, even if it differs. The reason: chewing does two jobs. It breaks food into small pieces, and it mixes them with saliva into a soft, slippery ball called a bolus. A dry biscuit breaks at once, so most of its chews are spent adding saliva. Water does that job quickly. A carrot is mostly water already, but its pieces are hard, so the chews are spent breaking them.
flow.think: Why do people in many places eat dry foods such as rusk, khakhra or murukku with tea, buttermilk or chutney?
flow.context: This is the last step of Dry or Wet. You say what your chew counts show about the biscuit and the carrot.

experiments.title: The Oil and Soap Bottles: what does bile do to fat?
experiments.question: Oil and water separate after shaking. Does a little dish soap keep the oil mixed into the water for longer? Does more soap work better than less?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After 15 minutes, which bottle will have the thickest layer of clear oil on top? Through which bottle will you still be able to read a newspaper? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use three bottles of the same size and shape. Put the same amount of water and the same amount of oil in each. The same person shakes every bottle 20 times, equally hard. Stand the bottles side by side and do not move them again. Only one thing changes: the number of drops of dish soap.
results_table: Bottle A, no soap: oil layer in millimetres, and can you read through it?

materials.item: clear bottles or jars of the same size with tight lids, such as 500 millilitre water bottles
water, half a steel tumbler (about 100 millilitres) for each bottle
cooking oil, 2 teaspoons for each bottle
dish wash liquid, 12 drops (or liquid hand wash, or shampoo)
a teaspoon, a ruler, a clock and a page of newspaper
paper and a pen for labels A, B and C

experiments.safety: Do not drink from the bottles. Pour them into the sink afterwards and wash the bottles with hot water and soap.
experiments.record: Draw a table with three rows, for 1, 5 and 15 minutes. For each bottle write how thick the clear oil layer is in millimetres. Also write yes or no: can you read a newspaper headline through the water?
experiments.context: In this experiment you shake oil and water in three bottles, with no soap, a little soap and more soap. You watch how long the oil stays mixed. Soap does to oil what bile does to fat in the small intestine.

setup.art: Three clear bottles labelled A, B and C, each one third full of water with a layer of yellow oil floating on top.
setup.caption: 1. Put half a tumbler of water and 2 teaspoons of oil in each bottle.

setup.art: A child squeezing drops of green dish wash liquid from a teaspoon into the bottle labelled C.
setup.caption: 2. Add no soap to A, 2 drops to B and 10 drops to C.

setup.art: A child shaking a closed bottle up and down with both hands.
setup.caption: 3. Close the lids tightly. Shake each bottle 20 times.

setup.art: Three bottles standing in front of a newspaper: the first with clear water and an oil layer on top, the second cloudy, the third milky white.
setup.caption: 4. Stand them in front of a newspaper. Look at 1, 5 and 15 minutes.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: oil layer 3 mm, can just read

flow.do: Put half a tumbler of water and 2 teaspoons of oil into bottle A. Let your child look. Then ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: The oil floats and does not mix. We will shake three bottles like this one. One has no soap, one has 2 drops and one has 10 drops. After 15 minutes, which will have the thickest oil layer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the oil on the water. Which bottle will stay mixed longest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think soap will or will not change anything?
good: Soap takes grease off plates.
Oil always floats, so it will come back.
More soap might hold more oil.

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Oil and Soap Bottles. You guess what soap will do to oil and water, before you test.

flow.do: Label the bottles A, B and C. Put the same water and oil into B and C. Add 2 drops of dish wash liquid to B and 10 drops to C. Close all three lids tightly.
flow.say: Every bottle gets the same water and the same oil. Only the soap changes. Count the drops with me.
flow.kid: Fill bottles B and C the same way. Add 2 drops to B. Add 10 drops to C.
flow.parent: Let drops fall from the tip of a teaspoon or straight from the nozzle. Ten drops are about half a teaspoon.
flow.context: In this step of the Oil and Soap Bottles you fill three bottles and add different amounts of soap.

flow.do: Your child shakes each bottle 20 times, equally hard. Stand the bottles side by side in front of an open newspaper. Start the clock. After 1 minute, measure the clear oil layer on top of each with the ruler. Try to read a headline through the lower part.
flow.say: Shake each one 20 times, just as hard each time. Now stand them down and do not touch them. After one minute we measure the oil on top.
flow.kid: Shake each bottle 20 times. Stand them by the newspaper. Measure after 1 minute.

check.q: In the Oil and Soap Bottles, why is each bottle shaken the same number of times?
options: So that only the soap differs
So that the oil gets warm
So that the lids stay tight
check.why: Harder shaking breaks oil into smaller drops. If one bottle were shaken more, we could not tell whether the soap or the shaking made the difference.

flow.parent: Bottle C may have foam on top. Foam is white and full of bubbles. The oil layer is clear and yellow. Measure only the oil.
flow.context: In this step of the Oil and Soap Bottles you shake the bottles and measure after 1 minute.

flow.do: At 5 minutes after shaking, measure the oil layers again without moving the bottles. Try the headline again. Record the results.
flow.say: Five minutes have passed. Measure the oil on top of each bottle. Can you read the headline through A? Through B? Through C?
flow.kid: Five minutes have passed. Measure the oil layers. Try to read the headline.
flow.context: In this step of the Oil and Soap Bottles you measure the oil layers 5 minutes after shaking.

flow.do: At 15 minutes after shaking, measure and record once more.
flow.say: Fifteen minutes now. This is the last measurement. Which bottle changed the most since the start? Which changed the least?
flow.kid: Fifteen minutes have passed. Measure once more. Which bottle changed least?
flow.parent: Use the waiting time for the term cards or the story.
flow.context: In this step of the Oil and Soap Bottles you take the last measurement, 15 minutes after shaking.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your table. Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it happened. Where did the oil in bottle C go?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you found. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The oil in bottle C did not vanish. Where is it?
good: It is in tiny drops, spread through the water.
The drops are too small to see one by one, so the water looks milky.

ask.q: An enzyme can only work on the outside of a drop of fat. Why would many tiny drops be digested faster than one big drop?
good: Tiny drops have much more outside in total.
The enzyme can reach more of the fat at once.

flow.parent: In most homes bottle A clears within a minute or two, with all its oil back on top. Bottle C stays milky for 15 minutes and much longer. Bottle B is usually in between. Write down what you really found. The reason: shaking breaks the oil into small drops, but in plain water the drops join up again. Soap coats each small drop, so the drops stay apart and stay hanging in the water. This is called emulsifying. Bile does the same to the fat in a meal. Bile is not soap, and it does not digest fat. It makes the fat into tiny droplets, and the enzymes from the pancreas then digest those droplets.
flow.think: Milk is tiny droplets of fat hanging in water. What might stop those droplets from joining up?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Oil and Soap Bottles. You say what your results show about soap, oil and water.

experiments.title: The Pleated Cloth Test: does a folded lining soak up more?
experiments.question: Two pieces of cloth cover the same space, 10 centimetres by 10 centimetres. One is a single flat layer. The other is four times as long and folded into pleats. How much more water does the pleated one take up?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Out of 10 teaspoons of water, how many will the flat cloth take up? How many will the pleated cloth take up? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Cut both pieces from the same old cotton banian or T-shirt. Both must cover the same square, 10 centimetres by 10 centimetres. Start each bowl with exactly 10 level teaspoons of water. Press each cloth under the water for a count of 10. Hold it above the bowl for a count of 20, so the drips fall back. Use a dry cloth for every try. Only one thing changes: how much cloth is packed into the square.
results_table: Teaspoons left in the bowl, try 1 and try 2
Teaspoons taken up (10 minus what is left)

materials.item: an old cotton banian or T-shirt to cut up (not a thick towel)
scissors and a ruler
safety pins or clothes pegs, to hold the pleats
small steel bowls (katori)
a teaspoon and a tumbler of water
a notebook page and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors and the safety pins.
experiments.record: Write how many teaspoons were left in the bowl after each cloth, for two tries. Take each number away from 10 to find how much the cloth took up.
experiments.context: In this experiment you compare a flat cloth with a pleated cloth that covers the same space. It is a model of the folds and villi that line the small intestine.

setup.art: Two flat squares of white cotton cloth and two long strips of the same cloth on a table, with a ruler and scissors.
setup.caption: 1. Cut 2 squares of 10 by 10 centimetres, and 2 strips of 10 by 40 centimetres.

setup.art: A long strip of cloth folded back and forth into four layers and held at two corners with safety pins.
setup.caption: 2. Fold each strip into four layers, like a fan. Pin it. Now it covers 10 by 10 centimetres.

setup.art: A child pressing a folded cloth under the water in a small steel bowl with the back of a teaspoon.
setup.caption: 3. Put 10 teaspoons of water in a bowl. Press the cloth under for a count of 10.

setup.art: A child holding a dripping cloth above the bowl, and then spooning the water left in the bowl into a tumbler while counting.
setup.caption: 4. Let the cloth drip for a count of 20. Count the teaspoons left in the bowl.

flow.do: Cut two squares of 10 by 10 centimetres and two strips of 10 by 40 centimetres from the banian. Fold each strip back and forth into four layers and pin two corners.
flow.say: Both kinds of cloth now cover the same square on the table. One has four times as much cloth packed into that square. Hold one of each.
flow.kid: Cut two squares and two long strips. Fold each strip into four layers. Pin them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pleated Cloth Test. You cut and fold the flat cloths and the pleated cloths.

flow.do: Put exactly 10 level teaspoons of water into each bowl. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Each bowl has 10 teaspoons of water. How many teaspoons will the flat cloth take up? How many will the pleated cloth take up? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put 10 teaspoons of water in each bowl. Guess how much each cloth takes. Why?

ask.q: Will the pleated cloth take four times as much, the same, or something in between? Why?
good: Four times, because there is four times as much cloth.
A bit less than four times, because the inside layers may not get fully wet in 10 seconds.
The same, because the square is the same size.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: In this step of the Pleated Cloth Test you guess how much water each cloth will take up.

flow.do: Press a flat cloth under the water in the first bowl for a count of 10. Lift it by a corner and hold it over the bowl for a count of 20. Put it aside. Count the teaspoons left in the bowl into a tumbler. Do the same with a pleated cloth in the second bowl. Then repeat both with fresh water and the dry cloths.
flow.say: Press it under and count to 10. Lift it and count to 20 while the drips fall back. Now spoon out the water that is left, and count the spoons.
flow.kid: Press the cloth under for 10 counts. Let it drip for 20. Count the spoons left.
flow.parent: If a cloth drinks up all 10 teaspoons, your cloth is thick. Start again with 20 teaspoons in both bowls.
flow.context: In this step of the Pleated Cloth Test you soak each cloth and count the teaspoons left.

flow.do: Work out how much each cloth took up. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Take each number away from 10. Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it happened. Both cloths covered the same square. Why did they take up different amounts?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you found. Say why it happened.

check.q: Why is the inside of the small intestine covered with folds and villi?
options: To slow the food to a stop
check.why: Digested food can only cross where it touches the wall. Folds and villi pack a large surface into a narrow tube. If you chose grinding, remember that villi are soft. Teeth and the stomach do the breaking.

flow.parent: A banian square usually takes up about 1 teaspoon, and the pleated cloth 3 or 4. Write down what you really found. The reason: water soaks in wherever it touches cloth. The pleated cloth has four times the surface in the same space. The small intestine uses the same plan. Its folds and villi give a tube 6 metres long about 30 square metres of lining. A cloth holds its water, but the gut passes food on to the blood. So the model shows only the idea of surface.
flow.think: Where else in your body is a large surface folded into a small space?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Pleated Cloth Test. You say what your results show about flat and folded linings.

activities.title: The Head-Down Swallow: does food need to fall?

materials.item: a ripe banana
a bed, a sofa or a mat to bend over
a tumbler of water and a drinking straw, if you have one

schedule.what: Swallow a chewed bite of banana with your head lower than your stomach, and notice where you feel it go.

activities.safety: A grown-up stays beside the child. Use a small bite, chewed until it is soft. Do not laugh or talk while swallowing. Do not try this with nuts, hard sweets or a full mouth.
activities.record: Write one sentence: what you thought would happen, and what happened.
activities.context: In this activity you swallow a bite of banana with your head lower than your stomach. It shows whether food falls into the stomach or is pushed there.

setup.art: A child sitting up straight and chewing a small bite of banana.
setup.caption: 1. Sit up. Chew a small bite of banana until it is soft. Do not swallow yet.

setup.art: A child standing and bending forward with her hands flat on a low bed, so that her head is lower than her stomach, with a grown-up beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Bend forward until your head is lower than your stomach.

setup.art: The same bent-over child with a dotted arrow drawn from her mouth along her neck towards her stomach.
setup.caption: 3. Swallow. Notice where you feel the bite go. Then stand up slowly.

flow.do: Ask the question below before anything else. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: When you swallow, how does the food get to your stomach? If your head were lower than your stomach, could you still swallow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How does food reach your stomach? Could you swallow with your head down? Why?

ask.q: What would happen to the bite if food simply fell into the stomach?
good: It would stay in my mouth.
It would fall back out.
It could not go up.

flow.parent: Many children say that food falls or slides down. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Head-Down Swallow. You guess whether a bite can reach the stomach when your head is down.

flow.do: Your child chews a small bite of banana until it is soft, sitting up. Then they stand, bend forward and put their hands on a low bed or the floor. The head must be lower than the stomach. They swallow, wait for a count of five and stand up slowly.
flow.say: Chew the banana well, and keep it in your mouth. Now bend down slowly until your head is below your tummy. Swallow. Where do you feel the bite going?
flow.kid: Chew a small bite well. Bend down, head below tummy. Swallow. Where does the bite go?
flow.parent: Stay close. If you have a straw, your child can then try three small sips of water in the same position. Stop if they feel dizzy.
flow.context: In this step of the Head-Down Swallow you swallow a chewed bite of banana with your head down.

flow.do: Sit together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what happened, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what happened, and why you think it happened. The bite went up to reach your stomach. What could have moved it?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what happened. Say why.

ask.q: Astronauts float, and so does their food. Can they swallow?
good: Yes, because the food pipe pushes the food.
Yes. Swallowing does not need falling.

flow.parent: The food pipe is a tube of muscle. A ring of muscle tightens just behind the bite and pushes it on. The squeezing travels along the tube as a wave, called peristalsis. Your child will model it in Squeeze It Along.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Head-Down Swallow. You say how a bite could reach the stomach with your head down.

activities.title: The Food Tube on the Floor: lay out 8 metres of wool

materials.item: wool or string in four colours if you have them, about 8 metres in all (strips of old cloth tied end to end also work)
a measuring tape or a ruler
scissors
four slips of paper and a pen, for labels

schedule.what: Cut wool for each part of a grown-up's food tube, join the pieces and lay them across the floor.

activities.record: A table with four rows: oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. Write the length of each and the time food spends there.
activities.context: In this activity you cut wool to the real length of each part of a grown-up's food tube. Then you lay the whole tube across the floor and compare it with your own height.

setup.art: Four pieces of wool in different colours on a floor: two short, one very long and one of medium length, each beside a paper label.
setup.caption: 1. Cut 25 centimetres, 25 centimetres, 6 metres and 1.5 metres of wool.

setup.art: A child tying the ends of two pieces of coloured wool together.
setup.caption: 2. Tie the four pieces end to end, in the order of the journey.

setup.art: A long line of wool running down a corridor and round a corner, with a child lying on the floor beside the first part of it.
setup.caption: 3. Lay the tube out. Lie beside it. How many of you would it take to match it?

flow.do: Before cutting, ask your child to show with their hands how long they think the whole food tube is. Mark their guess on the floor with two slippers.
flow.say: Food travels through one long tube, from your throat to your bottom. How long do you think that tube is in a grown-up? Show me on the floor. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How long is a grown-up's food tube? Mark your guess on the floor. Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Food Tube on the Floor. You guess how long a grown-up's food tube is.

flow.do: Measure and cut four pieces of wool. Cut 25 centimetres for the oesophagus and 25 centimetres for the stomach. Cut 6 metres for the small intestine and 1.5 metres for the large intestine. Write a label for each. Tie the pieces end to end in that order.
flow.say: Measure each part and cut it. The oesophagus is 25 centimetres. The stomach is 25 centimetres. The small intestine is 6 metres. The large intestine is 1.5 metres.
flow.kid: Measure and cut the four parts. Label each one. Tie them in order.
flow.parent: With one colour of wool, tie a knot or a paper flag where each part ends. With a short ruler, measure 1 metre of wool once. Then fold the wool against that metre six times.
flow.context: In this step of the Food Tube on the Floor you cut wool for each part of the food tube.

flow.do: Lay the whole tube out along a corridor or around a room. Your child lies down beside it. Mark how many of their body lengths it takes to match the tube.
flow.say: Here is the whole tube. Lie down beside the start. How many of you, head to toe, would match it? Which part is the longest?
flow.kid: Lay out the whole tube. Lie beside it. How many of you match it?

check.q: Which part of the food tube is the longest?
check.why: The small intestine is about 6 metres of the 8. It is called small because it is narrow. If you chose the large intestine, remember that 'large' describes its width. It is only about 1.5 metres long.

flow.parent: The whole tube is about 8 metres. A child of nine is about 1.3 metres tall, so about six children of that height, lying head to toe, would match the tube. Your child's own food tube is shorter than this one, because it grows with the body.
flow.context: In this step of the Food Tube on the Floor you lay out the wool tube beside your own body.

flow.do: Write the time food spends in each part on its label. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Now write the time on each label. The oesophagus takes less than 10 seconds. The stomach takes 2 to 4 hours. The small intestine takes 3 to 5 hours. The large intestine takes 1 to 2 days. All 8 metres fit in your belly. How can that be?
flow.kid: Write the time on each label. How do 8 metres fit inside a belly?

ask.q: How could a tube this long fit into a belly?
good: It is coiled up in loops.
It is folded back and forth.
It is narrow, so the loops pack closely.

flow.parent: Keep the wool. Your child can use the 6 metre piece in the challenge Six Metres in a Shoebox Lid.
flow.think: The longest part is the one where food is absorbed. Why might absorbing need so much length?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Food Tube on the Floor. You add the time food spends in each part, and ask how the tube fits in a belly.

activities.title: Squeeze It Along: a sleeve for a food pipe

materials.item: the sleeve of an old full-sleeved shirt or T-shirt, still on the shirt (or a long sock with the toe end cut off, or one leg of old leggings)
a lemon or a small ball that fits loosely in the sleeve
a ruler

schedule.what: Move a lemon through a sleeve by squeezing behind it, on the level and uphill.

activities.record: Write how many squeezes moved the lemon 25 centimetres on the level, and how many when the sleeve pointed uphill.
activities.context: In this activity you move a lemon through a cloth sleeve by squeezing behind it. It is a model of peristalsis, the wave of squeezing that moves food along the food pipe.

setup.art: A child holding a shirt sleeve out level with a round bump inside it near the shoulder end.
setup.caption: 1. Put the lemon into the sleeve at the shoulder end. Hold the sleeve level.

setup.art: A child's hand closed in a ring around the sleeve just behind the bump.
setup.caption: 2. Close your hand around the sleeve just behind the lemon. Squeeze.

setup.art: A child holding the cuff end of the sleeve high in the air and squeezing the lemon upwards through it.
setup.caption: 3. Now hold the cuff end up high. Squeeze the lemon uphill.

flow.do: Put the lemon in the sleeve at the shoulder end. Hold the sleeve level. Ask your child to move the lemon to the cuff without tipping the sleeve and without touching the lemon itself.
flow.say: The sleeve is a food pipe, and the lemon is a bite of food. Move the lemon to the other end. You may not tip the sleeve or hold the lemon. Where will you squeeze?
flow.kid: Put the lemon in the sleeve. Move it along without tipping. Where do you squeeze?
flow.context: This is the first step of Squeeze It Along. You work out how to move a lemon through a level sleeve.

flow.do: Your child makes a ring with thumb and fingers just behind the lemon and squeezes, hand after hand. Count the squeezes for 25 centimetres. Then they try squeezing in front of the lemon.
flow.say: Squeeze just behind the lemon, and then behind it again. Count your squeezes for 25 centimetres. Now squeeze in front of the lemon instead. Which way does it go?
flow.kid: Squeeze behind the lemon. Count the squeezes. Now squeeze in front. What happens?

check.q: In peristalsis, where does the food pipe squeeze to move food forward?
options: Just in front of the food
Along the whole pipe at once
check.why: A ring that tightens behind the food pushes it forward. A squeeze in front pushes it back. A squeeze everywhere at once would only trap the food.

flow.context: In this step of Squeeze It Along you squeeze behind the lemon, and then in front of the lemon.

flow.do: Hold the cuff end high, so that the sleeve points uphill. Your child squeezes the lemon up to the cuff. Then talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Now the sleeve points uphill. Can you still move the lemon to the top? What does this tell you about the Head-Down Swallow, when your bite of banana went up to your stomach?
flow.kid: Hold the sleeve uphill. Squeeze the lemon to the top. Does it still work?

ask.q: Your hand moved along the sleeve. What moves along a real food pipe?
good: The squeezing moves, as a wave.
One ring of muscle tightens, then the next ring, then the next.

flow.parent: In the real food pipe nothing travels along the outside. Each ring of muscle in the wall tightens in turn, and the ring ahead relaxes. In a grown-up the wave takes less than 10 seconds to cover 25 centimetres.
flow.context: This is the last step of Squeeze It Along. You squeeze the lemon uphill, as the food pipe did in the Head-Down Swallow.

projects.title: The Sweetcorn Clock: how long does the whole journey take?

materials.item: boiled sweetcorn kernels, 2 tablespoons (or half a cup of cooked beetroot if you have no corn)
a notebook page and a pencil
a clock

projects.safety: Only look before you flush. Do not touch. Wash your hands with soap afterwards, as you always do.

schedule.what: Eat the sweetcorn with dinner, write down the time and make your guess.
Look before you flush each time, and write what you see.
Look again, then work out how long the journey took.

projects.record: Write the day and time you ate the corn. Each time you pass faeces, write the day, the time, and yes or no: did you see corn skins? At the end, write the hours from eating to the first skins.
projects.context: In this three-day project you eat sweetcorn and watch for the skins in your faeces. The skin of a sweetcorn kernel is not digested. So it marks how long a meal takes to travel the whole food tube.

setup.art: A small steel bowl of yellow boiled sweetcorn kernels beside a dinner plate, and a clock on the wall showing half past seven.
setup.caption: 1. Eat 2 tablespoons of sweetcorn with dinner. Write down the time.

setup.art: A notebook page with rows for day and time, and a column of yes and no.
setup.caption: 2. Each time you go to the toilet, look before you flush. Write yes or no.

setup.art: A child counting on her fingers beside a notebook with two times circled.
setup.caption: 3. Count the hours from eating the corn to the first skins.

flow.do: Day 1. Choose a week when your child has eaten no sweetcorn for three days. At dinner, give 2 tablespoons of boiled sweetcorn. Ask them to chew some kernels only lightly. Write the day and the time. Ask for the guess and the reason.
flow.say: The thin skin of a sweetcorn kernel is one thing your enzymes cannot cut. So it comes out looking the same. How many hours do you think it will take? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Eat the sweetcorn. Write the time. How many hours will the skins take? Why?
flow.parent: If you have no sweetcorn, use half a cup of cooked beetroot. Beetroot colours the faeces dark red in most people, though not in everyone. Tell your child beforehand that the red is beetroot and not blood.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Sweetcorn Clock. You eat sweetcorn, write down the time and guess how long the journey will take.

flow.do: Day 2. Each time your child passes faeces, they look before flushing. They write the day, the time, and whether they saw yellow skins.
flow.say: Look before you flush. Do not touch. Do you see any yellow skins? Write the time, and yes or no. Then wash your hands with soap.
flow.kid: Look before you flush. Any yellow skins? Write the time. Wash your hands.
flow.wait: Do this the day after you eat the sweetcorn
flow.parent: Some children see skins the next morning. Others see none for two days. Both are healthy.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Sweetcorn Clock. You look for sweetcorn skins in your faeces and write down what you see.

flow.do: Day 3. Look again. When skins have been seen, count the hours from eating to the first skins. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why it took that long.
flow.say: Count the hours from dinner to the first skins. Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why you think it took that long. The skins went all the way through you. Did they ever pass into your blood?
flow.kid: Count the hours. Say what you guessed and what you found. Why so long?
flow.wait: Do this on the third day

ask.q: The corn spent only a few hours in the stomach and small intestine. Where did it spend the rest of the time?
good: In the large intestine.
The large intestine is the slowest part, 1 to 2 days.

ask.q: Why did the skins come out whole when the soft inside did not?
good: The skin is fibre, and our enzymes cannot cut it.
The inside is starch and sugar, which were digested and absorbed.

flow.parent: Most children see skins between 1 and 3 days after the meal. If you see none after 4 days, the skins were probably chewed too small to notice. Try again and chew a few kernels less. A regular time much longer than 3 days, with hard faeces, is worth mentioning to a doctor.
flow.think: The skins travelled the whole tube and never crossed its wall. Were they ever inside your body?
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Sweetcorn Clock. You work out how many hours the sweetcorn skins took to travel the food tube.

challenges.title: Six Metres in a Shoebox Lid: pack a small intestine
challenges.problem: A grown-up's small intestine is about 6 metres long, yet it fits in the belly. It must not kink, because a sharp fold would block the food. It must not slip about or knot when the person runs or jumps. Your problem is the same. Pack 6 metres of wool into a shoebox lid. It must have no sharp bends, stay in place and never knot.
constraints: All 6 metres must lie inside the lid. One end starts at the top left and the other ends at the bottom right.
No sharp bends. Every bend must be wide enough to go round a pencil.
The wool must stay in place when you stand the lid upright and shake it gently three times.
When you pull one end slowly, the whole length must come out with no knot.
You may use only tape, thread, paper and the wool.
materials: 6 metres of thick wool or soft string, such as the small intestine piece from the Food Tube on the Floor
a shoebox lid, or a steel plate about 25 centimetres across
a pencil, to check the bends
a sheet of paper and a little thread
general: Lay the wool in rows, back and forth across the lid, with a wide turn at each end.
Wind the wool in a flat spiral from the outside to the middle.
Tape the wool to the lid at every turn.
creative: Make two layers with a sheet of paper between them, as the belly has depth as well as width.
Tie each loop with a short thread to one pencil laid down the middle. The real small intestine hangs like this from a thin sheet called the mesentery.
Wind a double spiral, in to the middle and out again, so that both ends finish at the edge.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. It must pass all four tests: everything inside, no sharp bends, nothing moves when shaken, and no knot when pulled. Draw your design and write which test was hardest to pass.
challenges.context: In this challenge you pack 6 metres of wool into a shoebox lid without kinks or knots. It is the problem the body solves in fitting a small intestine about 6 metres long into the belly.

setup.art: A shoebox lid on a table beside a heap of thick wool, a pencil, sticky tape and a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. You have 6 metres of wool and a shoebox lid.

setup.art: Wool laid in neat rows back and forth inside the lid, with a pencil held in one of the turns to check its width.
setup.caption: 2. Pack the wool in. Check every bend with the pencil.

setup.art: A child holding the lid upright and shaking it, and then pulling one end of the wool out in a smooth line.
setup.caption: 3. Shake the lid three times. Then pull one end. Did it knot?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Let your child push the wool into the lid in a heap, shake it and pull one end.
flow.say: First, just push the wool in as a heap. Shake the lid and pull one end. What goes wrong? Now think about how the belly avoids that.
flow.kid: Push the wool in as a heap. Shake and pull. What goes wrong?

ask.q: What two things went wrong with the heap?
good: It knotted when I pulled.
It moved about or fell out when I shook the lid.
Some bends were sharp.

flow.context: This is the first step of Six Metres in a Shoebox Lid. You find out what goes wrong when the wool is packed as a heap.

flow.do: Your child chooses a plan and builds it. Check each bend with the pencil.
flow.say: Choose a plan and build it. Every bend must be wide enough for the pencil. How will you stop the loops from sliding?
flow.kid: Choose a plan and build it. Check each bend with the pencil.
flow.context: In this step of Six Metres in a Shoebox Lid you build your plan and check every bend.

flow.do: Test it. Stand the lid upright and shake it gently three times. Then pull one end slowly, all the way out. Record which tests it passed.
flow.say: Now we test. Shake three times. Did anything move? Pull one end slowly. Did it come out without a knot?
flow.kid: Shake the lid three times. Pull one end slowly. Did it pass?
flow.context: In this step of Six Metres in a Shoebox Lid you shake the lid and pull the wool.

flow.do: Change one thing to pass a failed test, or to use less tape. Test again. Then talk about the question below.
flow.say: Which test was hardest? Change one thing and try again. In your belly, no tape holds the loops. What might hold them?
flow.kid: Which test failed? Change one thing. Test again.

ask.q: What holds the loops of the real small intestine in place?
good: A thin sheet that joins every loop to the back of the belly.
Something like the threads tied to the pencil.

flow.parent: The real loops hang from a thin, fan-shaped sheet called the mesentery. The sheet joins every loop to the back wall of the belly. It also carries the blood vessels to the villi. Praise a clear account of what failed as much as a pass.
flow.context: This is the last step of Six Metres in a Shoebox Lid. You improve your packing and compare it with the real belly.

items.p: What is digestion for?
opts: Breaking food small enough to enter the blood
Keeping food warm inside the belly
Storing food until the next meal
items.why: Food pieces are far too big to pass through the gut wall. Digestion cuts them into small molecules that can cross into the blood.

items.p: Put these parts in the order that food passes through them.
items.why: Food goes from the mouth down the oesophagus to the stomach. Then it passes through the small intestine and last the large intestine.

items.p: The wave of squeezing that pushes food along the food tube is called ____.
items.why: In peristalsis a ring of muscle tightens just behind the food, and the tightening travels along the tube.

items.p: Food reaches the stomach only because it falls downwards.
items.why: False. Rings of muscle push the food. That is why you can swallow with your head down, and why astronauts can eat in space.

items.p: Match each part to its main job.
items.why: Each part does a different job. Breaking comes first, absorbing food comes in the small intestine, and taking back water comes last.

items.p: Which liquid in the mouth wets food and starts to digest starch?
items.why: Saliva makes food slippery and holds an enzyme that cuts starch into sugar. Bile and stomach acid are added further along.

items.p: Sort these. Does food pass through each one, or does it only send in a juice?
items.why: The liver and the pancreas are helper organs. They send bile and pancreatic juice into the small intestine, but food never enters them.

items.p: The small intestine is called small because it is short.
items.why: False. It is the longest part, about 6 metres in a grown-up. It is called small because it is narrow.

items.p: What do villi do?
opts: Absorb digested food into the blood
items.why: Villi are tiny fingers on the lining of the small intestine. Digested food passes through them into tiny blood vessels inside.

items.p: The yellow-green liquid made by the liver, which breaks fat into tiny droplets, is called ____.
items.why: Bile is stored in the gall bladder and flows into the small intestine. It works on fat as dish soap works on oil.

items.p: A dry biscuit needs many chews. A dipped biscuit needs few. Explain why in two sentences.
items.a: A bite can be swallowed only when the pieces are small and wet enough to stick together. A dry biscuit breaks easily, but the mouth must add saliva to wet it. Dipping adds the water at once, so fewer chews are needed.
items.why: A strong answer names both jobs of chewing, breaking and wetting. It says that the dry biscuit was waiting for wetting.

items.p: Explain how a bite of banana can reach your stomach when your head is lower than your stomach.
items.a: The oesophagus is a tube of muscle. A ring of muscle tightens behind the bite and pushes it forward, and the squeezing moves along the tube. A push works in any direction, so the bite can travel upwards.
items.why: A strong answer says that food is pushed by muscle. A push does not depend on which way is down.

items.p: Draw the food tube inside an outline of a body. Show the oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine.
items.a: One continuous tube. A straight oesophagus runs from the throat to a bag-shaped stomach under the ribs on the left. A long coiled small intestine fills the middle of the belly. A wider large intestine runs around the coils and ends at the bottom.
items.why: A strong drawing shows one unbroken tube, with the small intestine coiled and much longer than the rest.
items.art: A blank outline of a child's body from head to hips.

items.p: Is food in your stomach inside your body?

views.says: Yes. My stomach is under my skin and inside my belly, so the food in it is inside me.
No. The food tube is open at both ends, like a tunnel through me. Food is inside me only after it crosses the wall into my blood.
Both are fair ways to speak. The food is inside an organ of yours. But your body treats it as something from outside until it is absorbed.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what you know about the food tube. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that a sweetcorn skin passes through without crossing the gut wall. Another is that the body pours its own juices into the tube and controls what happens there.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses a fact about the food tube. Two such facts are its open ends and the wall that food must cross.

items.p: What are faeces mostly made of?
items.why: Faeces are about three quarters water. Much of the solid part is bacteria, and the rest is mostly fibre.

worksheets.title: Why each part works as it does

items.p: Dipping a raw carrot piece in water hardly changes its chew count. Why?
opts: The carrot needs breaking, not wetting
items.why: A carrot is mostly water already. Its chews are spent breaking hard pieces, and a dip in water does not break anything.

items.p: Why does the stomach let chyme out a little at a time?
opts: So the small intestine can deal with it
Because the stomach is too weak
So that food can go back up
items.why: The small intestine must cancel the acid, add bile and enzymes, and absorb the food. It can only handle a small amount at once.

items.p: Why does the stomach not digest its own wall?
opts: The wall is made of bone
items.why: A layer of slippery mucus keeps the acid and pepsin off the wall. The cells of the lining are also replaced every few days.

items.p: Blood from the small intestine goes to one organ first. Which one?
items.why: The liver receives the absorbed food first. It stores some sugar and breaks down many harmful molecules before the blood goes on.

items.p: Bile is an enzyme that digests fat.
items.why: False. Bile only breaks fat into tiny droplets. Enzymes from the pancreas then digest the droplets.

items.p: A person can live without a stomach.
items.why: True. Surgeons sometimes remove a stomach. The small intestine does most digestion, so the person can still digest food, eating small meals.

items.p: Sort each change. Is it mechanical digestion or chemical digestion?
items.why: Mechanical digestion makes smaller pieces of the same substance. Chemical digestion makes new, smaller molecules. Bile only makes smaller droplets of the same fat.

items.p: Three of these are added to food in the small intestine. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Bile, pancreatic juice and the wall's own enzymes all enter the small intestine. Saliva is added in the mouth.

items.p: A stomach squeezes 3 times a minute. How many times does it squeeze in 10 minutes?
items.why: 3 squeezes each minute for 10 minutes is 3 times 10, which is 30 squeezes.

items.p: Put these in order, to show what happens to the fat in a vada.
items: Teeth break the vada into pieces
The stomach churns the pieces into chyme
Bile breaks the fat into tiny droplets
Enzymes cut the fat into smaller units
a: Teeth break the vada into pieces
The stomach churns the pieces into chyme
Bile breaks the fat into tiny droplets
Enzymes cut the fat into smaller units
items.why: Fat must first be made into tiny droplets by bile. Only then can enzymes reach it. Absorbing comes last.

items.p: In the Oil and Soap Bottles, the bottle with 10 drops stayed milky. What does this show about bile?
items.a: Soap kept the oil in tiny droplets spread through the water. Bile does the same to fat in the small intestine. Tiny droplets have far more surface, so enzymes can digest the fat faster.
items.why: A strong answer says that the oil is still there as tiny droplets. It links droplets to more surface for enzymes.

items.p: With loose motions, food moves through the gut very fast. Explain why the child loses a lot of water.
items.a: The gut absorbs water as food passes slowly along it. When everything rushes through, there is too little time to absorb the water, so it leaves with the faeces. The child must drink water with sugar and salt to replace it.
items.why: A strong answer links speed to absorbing: less time in the tube means less water taken back.

items.p: A snake swallows an egg wider than the snake's own head. How does the egg move along the snake's body?
items.a: Muscles in the wall of the snake's food tube squeeze just behind the egg and push it along. This is peristalsis, the same way your own food pipe moves a bite.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of squeezing behind the food, and sees that one idea explains both animals.

items.p: An old rule says: chew every bite 32 times. Three people talk about it.

views.says: Chew every bite 32 times. Well-chewed food is easy on the stomach, and you enjoy the taste for longer.
No single number fits. A banana is ready in about ten chews and a carrot needs thirty. The mouth knows when a bite is ready.
The stomach churns food anyway, so I can swallow big pieces and let the stomach do the work.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from your own chew counts in Dry or Wet. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. The chew counts in Dry or Wet differ from food to food, which supports the scientist. The grandmother is right that small, wet pieces are digested more easily. The child is partly right that the stomach churns. But the stomach has no teeth, and large pieces can make a person choke.
items.why: A strong answer uses the child's own numbers, and takes what is true in another view seriously.

items.p: Label four parts on this picture of the food tube: oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine.
a: Oesophagus: the straight tube from the throat down through the chest
Stomach: the bag under the ribs on the left side
Small intestine: the narrow coiled tube in the middle of the belly
Large intestine: the wider tube that frames the small intestine
items.why: The parts come in the order of the journey. The small intestine is narrow and coiled, and the large intestine is wider and runs around it.
items.art: An outline of a body with the food tube drawn inside it and four blank label lines.

items.p: René de Réaumur fed a kite meat inside metal tubes. The meat still dissolved. What did this show?
opts: Juices digest food without any grinding
items.why: The tube could not be crushed, so nothing ground the meat. Something liquid entered the tube and dissolved it. Digestion is chemical as well as mechanical.

items.p: A dog's intestine still squeezed food along after its nerves to the brain were cut. What does this show?
opts: The gut has its own nerve net
The brain is not needed for anything
items.why: The intestine sensed the food and squeezed behind it without the brain. The nerve net in the gut wall runs peristalsis.

items.p: A smooth tube would have half a square metre of lining. The small intestine has 30. What makes the difference?
items.why: The tube is the same length. Folds, villi and tiny bumps on the cells pack about 60 times as much surface into it.

items.p: Fibre cannot be cut by human enzymes. What happens to it in the large intestine?
opts: Gut bacteria feed on the fibre
It goes back to the stomach
items.why: Gut bacteria break down part of the fibre and make gases and some vitamins. The rest leaves in the faeces and helps them hold water.

items.p: Most stomach ulcers are caused by eating spicy food.
items.why: False. Barry Marshall and Robin Warren showed that most ulcers come from a bacterium called Helicobacter pylori. Some pain medicines cause ulcers too.

items.p: Your stomach can start making gastric juice before any food reaches it.
items.why: True. The smell, sight or taste of food sends a message along nerves from the brain. The stomach then starts making juice.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they showed.
pairs: Meat dissolves inside a tube that cannot be crushed
William Beaumont, with Alexis St. Martin
Gastric juice digests meat outside the body
The intestine squeezes food along by its own nerves
A drink of sugar and salt saves people with cholera
items.why: Each finding answered a different question. Is digestion chemical? What does the stomach's juice do? Who runs the gut? How can we help the gut absorb water?

items.p: Food takes about 4 hours to pass through 6 metres of small intestine. How many metres is that each hour?
items.why: 6 metres in 4 hours is 6 divided by 4, which is one and a half metres each hour. That is slower than a snail.

items.p: The thick liquid that leaves the stomach is called ____.
items.why: The stomach churns food with gastric juice for 2 to 4 hours. The result is a thick, sour liquid called chyme.

items.p: A child says: 'Milk is a liquid, so it needs no digesting.' Is this right? Explain.
items.a: It is not right. Milk holds protein, fat and milk sugar, and their molecules are too big to cross the gut wall. Enzymes must cut them first. Being liquid only means that milk needs no chewing.
items.why: A strong answer separates the size of the pieces you can see from the size of the molecules. Digestion is about molecules.

items.p: Plan a fair test: does a meal with more fat stay longer in the stomach? Say what you would change.
items.a: Eat two meals of the same size at the same time of day. One has little fat and one has more. Change only the amount of fat. Note the time when you first feel hungry again after each meal. Repeat on several days.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the fat. It keeps the size of the meal and the time of day the same, and repeats the test. Feeling hungry is a rough measure, and a strong answer may say so.

items.p: Why is a cut-up vada a poor model of what bile does? Why is oil shaken with soap better?
items.a: Cutting a vada makes smaller pieces of food, which is the job of teeth. Bile works on liquid fat and keeps it in tiny droplets that do not join up again. Oil shaken with soap shows exactly that.
items.why: A strong answer says what a model must show: tiny droplets of fat that stay apart in water.

items.p: The Pleated Cloth Test is a model of villi. Name one way it is like villi and one way it differs.
items.a: It is like villi because folding packs more surface into the same space, so more is taken up. It is unlike villi because a cloth only holds the water. Villi pass the food on into the blood, so they never fill up.
items.why: A strong answer gives a true likeness about surface and a true difference, such as blood carrying the food away.

items.p: Dr Beaumont tested digestion for years through a hole in the stomach of Alexis St. Martin. Was this fair?

views.says: I treated his wound when everyone thought he would die. I gave him a home and paid him. What I learned has helped doctors and patients ever since.
I was poor and could not read the paper I signed. The tests made me sore and sick, and I wanted to go home to my family. My stomach is in his book, but my name is hardly known.
The knowledge is real and useful. But today a patient must understand a test and be free to say no at any time. We should also name St. Martin whenever we name Beaumont.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A strong answer weighs the knowledge gained against St. Martin's pain and his lack of free choice. It may say that both men should be credited.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A strong answer does not treat the knowledge as worthless, and does not treat St. Martin's wishes as unimportant.

items.p: Draw three villi as they would look under a microscope. Show the blood vessels inside, and show sugar passing in.
items.a: Three finger shapes standing side by side on a wall. Inside each one are thin red and blue lines for blood vessels. Small dots outside the fingers have arrows pointing through the surface into the vessels.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the food crosses the surface of the villus and enters the blood inside it.
items.art: A blank box with a straight line along the bottom for the wall of the intestine.

quiz.p: Why must food be digested before the body can use it?
opts: Its pieces are too big for the blood
It is too heavy to carry
quiz.why: Only small molecules can cross the gut wall. Digestion cuts large food molecules into small ones.

quiz.p: Which list gives the journey of food in the right order?
opts: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine
Mouth, stomach, oesophagus, large intestine, small intestine
Mouth, liver, stomach, small intestine, large intestine
Mouth, oesophagus, small intestine, stomach, large intestine
quiz.why: The oesophagus leads to the stomach. The small intestine comes before the large intestine. Food never passes through the liver.

quiz.p: Which two organs help digestion although food never passes through them?
quiz.why: The liver makes bile and the pancreas makes pancreatic juice. Both juices flow into the small intestine through a small tube.

quiz.p: What are the two jobs of chewing?
opts: Breaking food small and wetting it
quiz.why: Teeth break the food, and saliva wets the pieces so they stick together and slide. A bite needs both before it can be swallowed.

quiz.p: How does a bite move along the oesophagus?
opts: It falls under its own weight
Air from the lungs blows it
quiz.why: This squeezing is peristalsis. It pushes food in any direction, so it does not depend on falling.

quiz.p: An astronaut floating in space is able to swallow food.
quiz.why: True. Peristalsis pushes the food to the stomach. Nothing needs to fall.

quiz.p: Which of these is a job of the stomach?
opts: Taking back most of the water
quiz.why: The stomach stores, churns and adds acid and pepsin. Most absorbing happens in the small intestine, and bile comes from the liver.

quiz.p: What does bile do to the fat in a meal?
quiz.why: Bile keeps fat in tiny droplets, as soap did to the oil in the Oil and Soap Bottles. Enzymes then digest the droplets.

quiz.p: Where is nearly all digested food absorbed into the blood?
quiz.why: The villi of the small intestine absorb sugars, amino acids and fats. The large intestine absorbs mainly water and salts.

quiz.p: What is the main job of the large intestine?
quiz.why: The large intestine absorbs water and salts from what is left. Its bacteria also feed on fibre.

quiz.p: About how long does a meal take to travel the whole food tube?
quiz.why: The oesophagus takes seconds and the stomach and small intestine take hours. The large intestine takes 1 to 2 days, so the whole journey takes 1 to 3 days.

quiz.p: A grown-up's food tube is about 8 metres long. Which part makes up most of that length?
quiz.why: The small intestine is about 6 metres of the 8. The large intestine is about 1.5 metres, and the oesophagus and stomach are about 25 centimetres each.

applications: Oral rehydration solution, or ORS, is water with sugar and salt in set amounts. Sugar helps the small intestine absorb salt and water, so ORS saves children with loose motions.
Doctors can ask a patient to swallow a camera the size of a large tablet. Peristalsis carries it through the whole food tube while it takes pictures.
For an X-ray of the food tube, the patient drinks a white liquid that blocks X-rays. Doctors then watch the swallow and the waves of squeezing on a screen.
Some tablets have a coat that stomach acid cannot dissolve. The coat dissolves only in the small intestine, so the medicine is released there.
Cooks pound, grind, soak and ferment food. Idli batter is ground and fermented, so part of the work of breaking down is done before the first bite.
Vets treat cows whose rumen has stopped moving. The rumen is the first and biggest part of a cow's stomach. A vet listens to the belly, because a healthy rumen squeezes once or twice every minute.

open_questions.q: Do the bacteria in the gut change how we feel and think?
open_questions.why_open: In mice, gut microbes change behaviour. In people the studies are small and often disagree, and nobody yet knows how strong the effect is.
One idea is that it keeps a store of helpful bacteria for refilling the gut after an illness. People live well without an appendix, so the idea is hard to test.

open_questions.q: Why do some people's guts move food much faster or slower than others'?
open_questions.why_open: Food, water, exercise, microbes and the gut's own nerves all play a part. Scientists cannot yet predict one person's time from these.

open_questions.q: How do the hundreds of millions of nerve cells in the gut wall work together?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can describe single reflexes such as peristalsis. How the whole net senses a meal and plans hours of work is still being mapped.

open_questions.q: How does the gut tell food from a harmful microbe, when both arrive the same way?
open_questions.why_open: The gut wall holds a large share of the body's defence cells. How they learn to leave food and helpful bacteria alone is only partly understood.
