maths.problem: In Dry or Wet, a dry half biscuit took 22 chews and then 20 chews. A dipped half biscuit took 9 and then 8. Find the middle value for each kind of bite. About how many times as many chews did the dry bite need?
maths.answer: Dry: 21 chews. Dipped: 8 and a half chews. The dry bite needed about two and a half times as many.
maths.explain: 22 and 20 add to 42, and half of 42 is 21. 9 and 8 add to 17, and half of 17 is 8 and a half. Two lots of 8 and a half make 17. Two and a half lots of 8 and a half make about 21, which is the dry count. So the dry bite needed about two and a half times as many chews.
maths.context: In Dry or Wet you count how many chews a bite needs before it is ready to swallow. These are made-up counts for a dry biscuit and a dipped biscuit.
maths.why_maths: Two tries rarely give the same count. The value halfway between them is a fairer number to compare.

maths.problem: In Dry or Wet, a dry carrot piece took 30 chews and then 28. A dipped carrot piece took 29 and then 27. Did dipping change the carrot? Explain how you can tell.
maths.answer: No, there is no clear change.
maths.explain: The dry tries differ from each other by 2 chews. The dry and dipped counts differ by only 1 chew. A difference smaller than the difference between two tries of the same bite could be chance.
maths.context: In Dry or Wet you count the chews for a raw carrot piece, dry and dipped in water. These are made-up counts.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a difference with the spread between repeated tries tells you whether the difference means anything.

maths.problem: In the Food Tube on the Floor, the four pieces of wool were 25, 25, 600 and 150 centimetres long. How long is the whole tube? What fraction of it is the small intestine?
maths.answer: 800 centimetres, which is 8 metres. The small intestine is three quarters of it.
maths.explain: 25 + 25 + 600 + 150 = 800 centimetres. The small intestine is 600 out of 800. Divide both by 200 to get 3 out of 4.
maths.context: In the Food Tube on the Floor you cut wool for each part of a grown-up's food tube.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows at once how much of the journey belongs to the part that absorbs food.

maths.problem: A smooth tube the size of the small intestine would have half a square metre of lining. The real lining has 30 square metres. How many times as much is that?
maths.explain: The smooth tube has half a square metre of lining. Each whole square metre holds two halves. So 30 square metres hold 30 times 2 halves, which is 60 halves. That means the real lining is 60 times as big as the smooth one.
maths.context: In the Pleated Cloth Test a folded cloth takes up more water than a flat cloth covering the same space. Folds and villi do the same for the small intestine.
maths.why_maths: Dividing shows how much the folding adds, which a picture of villi alone cannot tell you.

maths.problem: In the Pleated Cloth Test, the flat cloth took up 1 teaspoon. The pleated cloth has 4 times as much cloth, but it took up 3 teaspoons. Give one reason why it took less than 4.
maths.answer: The inside layers may not have been fully wet after a count of 10.
maths.explain: Four times the cloth could hold 4 teaspoons. Water reaches the outer layers first. The inner layers are pressed together and get less water in a short time. A longer soak would bring the number closer to 4.
maths.context: In the Pleated Cloth Test you soak a flat cloth and a cloth folded into four layers. You count the teaspoons of water each takes up. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Work out what the number should be, and compare it with what you found. That shows where a model falls short.

maths.problem: In the Sweetcorn Clock, the corn was eaten on Monday at 7:30 in the evening. The first skins were seen on Wednesday at 7:00 in the morning. How long did the journey take?
maths.explain: From Monday 7:30 in the evening to Tuesday 7:30 in the evening is 24 hours. From then to Wednesday 7:00 in the morning is 11 hours and 30 minutes. 24 hours and 11 and a half hours make 35 hours and 30 minutes.
maths.context: In the Sweetcorn Clock you eat sweetcorn and note the time when the skins first appear in your faeces. These times are made up.
maths.why_maths: Counting across two nights is easy to get wrong. Splitting the time into a full day and a remainder keeps it right.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many doctors thought the stomach worked only by grinding, as a mill grinds grain. Others thought food was cooked or rotted there. In 1752 the French scientist René de Réaumur tested this with a kite. A kite is a bird of prey who brings up what she cannot digest. He put meat inside small metal tubes with open ends and let her swallow them. The tubes came back unharmed, so nothing had ground the meat. Yet the meat was partly dissolved. Some juice had done it. In Italy, Lazzaro Spallanzani repeated such tests on many animals. He even swallowed small linen bags of food himself. In 1822, at a trading post in North America, a young man named Alexis St. Martin was shot in the side. The wound healed with a hole that led into his stomach. From 1825 to 1833 the army doctor William Beaumont lowered pieces of food into the hole on silk threads. Later he pulled them out to look. He collected gastric juice and watched it digest meat in a warm glass tube. St. Martin was poor, and he did not always want to be tested.
how_we_found_out.who: René de Réaumur in France, Lazzaro Spallanzani in Italy, and William Beaumont with Alexis St. Martin in North America
how_we_found_out.when: Réaumur's tests were in 1752. Spallanzani published in 1780. St. Martin was shot in 1822, and Beaumont's book came out in 1833.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the stomach digests only by grinding, or by cooking or rotting the food. Réaumur showed that meat dissolved inside a metal tube that nothing could grind. Beaumont showed that gastric juice digests meat outside the body.
how_we_found_out.art: A bird of prey on a perch in an old study, with a small metal tube and a piece of meat on a table beside a man in eighteenth-century clothes.

roots.context: In this unit you followed a bite of food along a tube about 8 metres long. Here we ask where the food stops being food and starts being you.

deep_truth.truth: In the Sweetcorn Clock, the skins of the corn came out looking as they did when they went in. They travelled the whole food tube and never passed through its wall. The food tube is one long passage, open at the mouth and at the anus. So food you have swallowed is still outside your body until it crosses the gut wall.
deep_truth.habit: We say food is 'inside us' as soon as we swallow it, because it is under the skin. The food tube is a passage through the body. Only what crosses its wall enters the blood and the cells.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Sweetcorn Clock, the skins pass through whole in 1 to 3 days. In the Food Tube on the Floor, the wool is one unbroken line with two open ends. Digestion exists because whole food cannot cross the gut wall, and only small molecules can.

three.who_am_i: Your body is built from what crossed your gut wall. The sugar in your muscles this evening was part of a banana or a bowl of rice this morning.
three.what_is_life: Every animal, including you, takes other living things apart and builds a body from the pieces. A cow, a snake and a child all do this along a tube of muscle.
three.what_is_this_world: Rice, dal and fish are all cut into the same few kinds of small molecules. Every living thing is built from that same small set of building units, so what eats and what is eaten share the same ones.

roots.thread: A bite of idli is made of rice and urad dal. The rice and the dal plants grew from sunlight, water, air and soil. In your small intestine the idli is cut into sugars and amino acids. They cross the wall of a villus, and after that they are your blood, your muscle and your warmth. Many sages taught that the eater and the eaten are one. The science here says something close and plain. Your body and your food are built from the same kinds of molecules. That is why one can become the other.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu that food, when eaten, divides into three. The coarsest part becomes faeces, the middle part becomes flesh, and the finest part becomes mind.
teachings.link: This is an old account of the same journey: part of a meal leaves, and part becomes the body. Today we would say that what is absorbed also feeds the brain. The text's 'three parts' are a teaching, and not a measurement.

teachings.teaching: The verse ends in a song: 'I am food, I am food, I am food. I am the eater of food.'
teachings.link: Everything you digest was alive, and your own body will feed other living things one day. The verse says in a song what a food chain says in a diagram. The Upanishad means it as an insight about the self, which science does not test.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, 'interbeing', in The Heart of Understanding (1988)
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you can see the cloud, the rain and the forest there. Nothing exists by itself alone.
teachings.link: Look at your hand in the same way. Your hand was built from what crossed your gut wall. So the idli is in your hand, and so are the paddy field and the rain that grew the rice.

science.text: The lining of your small intestine is worn away and replaced every few days. The new cells are built from the food that the old cells absorbed.
All living things use the same kinds of sugars, fats and amino acids, because all share one ancestor. That is why almost any living thing can be food for some other.

Whether the bacteria in the gut count as part of 'you' is argued. Some biologists treat a human and their microbes as one unit, called a holobiont. Others say the microbes are separate beings who live with us.

other_view.who: Many doctors, and people who study anatomy
other_view.view: Calling the inside of the gut 'outside the body' is only a way of speaking about shape. The gut is an organ of yours. Your body pours 7 litres of its own juices into it each day and controls what happens there. On this view a swallowed bite is inside you from the moment you swallow. Digestion is your body working on what it already holds.

practice.title: One slow bite
practice.say: Take one small bite of fruit. Chew slowly and notice the pieces getting smaller and wetter. Notice the moment when the bite feels ready. Now swallow, and follow the bite down for as long as you can feel it. Put your hand on your belly. The work goes on there for a day or more. Sit quietly for five breaths.
practice.kid: Take one small bite. Chew slowly. Notice when it feels ready. Swallow, and follow it down. Put a hand on your belly. Breathe five times.

ask: In the Sweetcorn Clock, the corn skins travelled through you and never crossed the gut wall. Were they ever inside you?
The sugar from this morning's breakfast is now in your blood. Is it still breakfast, or is it you?
You chose when to swallow. After that, your gut did the work for a day. Who was doing it?

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step, but not yet done at home. Dry or Wet (core) needs 2 plain biscuits, one raw carrot and water. Most children need about half as many chews for a dipped biscuit as for a dry one, and the carrot hardly changes. Chew counts differ a lot from child to child, so the steps say to record what really happens. The Head-Down Swallow (core) needs a ripe banana and a grown-up beside the child. Use a small, well-chewed bite, and stop if the child feels dizzy. The Oil and Soap Bottles (core) needs three clear bottles with tight lids, oil and dish wash liquid. Bottle A clears in a minute or two and bottle C stays milky far longer. Bottle B varies with the brand of soap, and foam on bottle C must not be measured as oil. The Food Tube on the Floor (core) needs about 8 metres of wool, string or cloth strips, and a corridor or a room to go round. The Pleated Cloth Test works best with an old cotton banian. A thick towel drinks all the water, and the step says what to do then. The Sweetcorn Clock takes up to three days. Some children see nothing because they chew very well, and the step says to try again. Cooked beetroot works in place of corn for most people, but not all. Squeeze It Along needs an old sleeve or sock and a lemon. Six Metres in a Shoebox Lid is hard with thick wool in one layer, and that difficulty is part of the challenge. No part needs a garden or an animal. Facts to treat with care: the lengths of the gut are the usual rounded figures for a grown-up, and they vary from about 3 to 7 metres for the small intestine. The times in each part vary from person to person. The surface of about 30 square metres is from Helander and Fändriks (2014), and many older books give a much larger figure. Hundreds of millions of gut nerve cells and tens of trillions of gut bacteria are estimates. The Upanishad verses are given as paraphrases. The three videos have no address yet.
